title: The Insufficiency of the Law
english: The blessed David said that in his ecstasy, he proclaimed that every man is a liar, a statement that also applies to God, to us, and to all others.
For instance, when it comes to righteousness, it can be said, without straying from the truth, that God is righteous, while every man is unrighteous, as stated in Romans 3:4.
If our unrighteousness serves to establish God's righteousness, then this idea has given rise to a pretext for slander, which originated from the time when the sons of Israel returned from Babylon.

After their return, the sons of Israel were commanded by Cyrus to rebuild the temple, fulfill their vows, and offer sacrifices, but they became complacent, pretending to be poor and suffering from the hardships of captivity, and were being tempered by moderate educations and the scarcity of fruits and rains, which made them wise.

Despite these challenges, they remained unshakeable and even blessed the foreigners and those who did not serve God, as if they were living in prosperity, and claimed that these people were more blessed than themselves.

The prophet Malachi spoke out against them, saying, 'You have made your words heavy upon me, says the Lord, and have said: In what way have we spoken against you?' (Malachi 2:4), and, 'Say, and what more is there, that we kept His guardrails and went humbly before the face of the Lord Almighty? And now we bless strangers, and they are building houses!' (Malachi 3:14-15).
They withstood God and were saved, and those who feared the Lord discussed these things among themselves, with each one speaking to his neighbor, and the Lord listened and responded.

Because of this, some Jews were inclined to say, daring to presume that they could say, 'Let us do evil so that good things might come,' having declared that the judgment is a full measure of righteousness, and addressing those who were reproaching them for such ideas.

But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed, and it is known that certain men were considered righteous, walking in the commandments and judgments of Christ, blameless, and the blessed Paul said that he himself had also become blameless according to the righteousness that is in the law.

However, being blameless in this regard does not mean that one has already performed the deeds that will make him bright and without reproach, and the blessed Paul said again that he had reckoned all things in the law as loss and as equal refuse, seeking instead the excellence of the knowledge of Christ.

The law, however, continues to condemn those who transgress, and it is clear that if there is glory in the ministry of condemnation, then the ministry of righteousness must abound even more in glory, as stated in 2 Corinthians 3:9.
Since there is a greater commandment within the law, it is inevitable that even the most precise law-keeper will stumble and become a transgressor of the law in some way.

The noble disciples have truly and clearly judged the law to be a burden, saying, 'Now then, why are you testing God by placing a yoke upon the necks of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?' (Acts 15:10).
translator_notes: The text begins mid-sentence with the attribution to David.
The Greek text contains some OCR/typographical issues, which were interpreted based on context.
The numbers '1' and '178' appear to be page/line markers and were skipped.
The phrase 'vain one' translates the Greek concept of someone who serves God in a self-righteous manner.
The phrase 'guardrails' refers to the boundaries or precepts of God.
The phrase 'equal refuse' refers to considering all things in the law as worthless or of no value.

title: Justification by Grace Through Faith
english: When the Greeks were under sin because they had not known the creator, and the Jews were guilty as transgressors of the law, it was absolutely necessary that the justifying Christ should come for those living on earth. We have been justified not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to the abundance of his mercy. He himself long ago spoke through the prophets saying, 'I am the one who wipes out your iniquities, and I will by no means remember them.' The justifying grace overflows equally into all—I say both Jews and Greeks—for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.

Glory of God would reasonably be considered as that which neither comes from knowing nor from being born to sin. Afterward, certainly, every created thing is subject to the exaltations of divinity, for we have slipped and even some of the angels have fallen. Yet it pleased God the Father to sum up all things in Christ the justifying one, freely by his grace. He has been set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood, since he made his own blood an exchange for the life of all. He has saved those under heaven and has made the Father in the heavens gracious and favorable toward us.

Where then is boasting? It has been excluded. For who indeed, or concerning what, will anyone boast? All are in need and have turned aside from the straight way, and no one at all exists who completely does good. Therefore boasting is excluded—it has been cast out and destroyed, having no place among us. It was excluded by the forgiveness of past sins, by which we have been enriched, being justified by mercy and grace freely in Christ.

Do we then nullify the law by faith? Certainly not! For the God of all spoke to the wondrous Moses, saying: 'I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers, and I will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him. And whoever does not heed whatever words that prophet speaks in my name, I will require it from him.'

How then do we not uphold the law through faith, as we approach the word that comes from him? And this prophet is called Emmanuel because of his humanity, who, in the order of Moses, serves as a mediator between God and humanity.
Indeed, the law was given in shadows, but the true form of reality is revealed in the travail that brings it forth; truth does not do away with the foreshadowing, but makes it more clearly seen.

For if Abraham had been justified by works, he would have had something to boast about—but not before God. Yet we must consider the claim that those who engage in much discussion about Abraham our forefather should remember what was said to one of the holy disciples: that faith without works is dead.
But he adds to this: 'Do you want to know, O vain person, that faith apart from works is dead?' Abraham our father was not justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac upon the altar.

The author's voice is polemical and hortatory, using rhetorical questions and direct address ('O empty man'), which is reflected in the English tone.

title: Redemption through Christ's Incarnation and Victory over Death
english: Our Lord Jesus Christ has made plain the Father’s love beyond price, showing it to us in the completion of the fleshly dispensation and in the suffering of the cross, even as he declared, 'For God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.' (John 3:16)
He truly gave his own Son for our sake.

We have been redeemed; we have been freed from death and sin. The Word became flesh and dwelt in us not for any other reason, but so that, having endured the death of the flesh, he might triumph over every ruler and authority and abolish the one who holds the power of death— that is, the devil— and thus destroy corruption and put away the sin that tyrannizes over us.

In this way he declares inactive henceforth that ancient curse which human nature endured in Adam, as the firstfruit of the race and as the root of the first, for Adam, having transgressed the commandment, became guilty before his Maker and thereby became both accursed and held fast by death.
Yet the Lord of all again brought destruction upon those utterly lost.
For the Son came down from heaven, taking away sins, justifying the ungodly through faith, transforming human nature into incorruption as God, and bringing it back to the beginning.

Our Lord Jesus Christ truly demonstrated the Father's love toward us, making it evident through the end of the fleshly economy and the passion on the cross, saying, 'For God so loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.' (John 3:16)

He truly gave his own Son for us, we are redeemed, we have been freed from death and sin, not because the flesh of the Word came and dwelt in us for any other reason, but so that having endured the death of the flesh, he might triumph over rulers and authorities and abolish him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and might destroy corruption and put away the sin that tyrannizes over us, and thus declare inactive henceforth that ancient curse which human nature endured in Adam as the firstfruit of the race and as the root of the first, for Adam having transgressed the commandment became guilty before his Maker, and thereby became both accursed and held fast by death, yet the Lord of all again brought destruction upon those utterly lost, for the Son came down from heaven, removing sins, justifying the ungodly through faith, transforming human nature into incorruption as God, and bringing it back to the beginning.
